column1: In an SSMS graphical SELECT plan, rows generally flow {{c1::right to left}}, toward the root SELECT operator.
column2:
The left side is where rows reach the root operator for the statement. Follow the arrows from operators that read data toward the operators that consume those rows.
Review source

column1: In a graphical plan in SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS), wider arrows indicate {{c1::more rows flowing between operators}}.
column2:
Wider arrows indicate more rows, not more elapsed time. Inspect the arrow properties for the row count, and distinguish estimates from runtime counts when reading an actual plan.
Review source

column1: Operator cost percentages in an actual execution plan remain {{c1::optimizer estimates}}, not measured percentages of elapsed time.
column2:
The optimizer computes these percentages from estimated costs. Running the query adds evidence such as actual rows, but it does not turn the cost percentages into operator timing measurements.
Review source

column1: Generate estimated XML plans without executing subsequent queries with {{c1::SET SHOWPLAN_XML ON;}}
column2:
SQL Server compiles the statements and returns their estimated XML plans instead of running them. Run the SET command in its own batch. Turn it off before running statements normally.
Review source

column1: Execute queries and return XML plans with runtime information using {{c1::SET STATISTICS XML ON;}}
column2:
This command runs the subsequent statements and returns XML with runtime details. Unlike SHOWPLAN_XML, it executes writes as well as reads. Turn it off after collecting the needed plans.
Review source

column1: For a sys.dm_exec_query_stats row with executions, average CPU time is {{c1::total_worker_time / execution_count}}.
column2:
Divide the total CPU consumed by the number of completed executions represented by the row. The result excludes time spent waiting for resources because it measures CPU, not elapsed time.
Review source

Convert the reported value to milliseconds by dividing by 1,000. The view reports microseconds, but the underlying measurement is accurate only to milliseconds, so extra digits do not imply extra precision.
Review source

column1: To retrieve batch text from a query statistics row aliased qs, apply {{c1::sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle)}}.
column2:
The SQL handle identifies the batch text. If the batch contains several statements, use the start and end offsets to identify the statement associated with the selected statistics row.
Review source

column1: To retrieve a cached XML plan from a statistics row aliased qs, apply {{c1::sys.dm_exec_query_plan(qs.plan_handle)}}.
column2:
The plan handle identifies the compiled plan in the cache. The XML describes the chosen operators and estimates, not actual row counts from a specific execution.
Review source

column1: In sys.dm_exec_requests, a positive {{c1::blocking_session_id}} identifies the session blocking the request.
column2:
A positive ID names a session you can look up to continue tracing the blocking chain. A negative value can represent a special condition rather than a normal session.
Review source

column1: In sys.dm_exec_requests, {{c1::wait_type}} identifies the kind of resource wait.
column2:
The wait type describes the kind of resource the request is waiting for. The wait_time column measures how long this current wait has lasted, not how long the whole request has run.
Review source

column1: For a sys.dm_exec_query_stats row with executions, total_logical_reads / execution_count estimates {{c1::logical reads per execution}} on average.
column2:
A logical read counts a page accessed through the buffer cache, whether or not a disk read was needed. Compare the per-run average with the amount of data the query returns.
Review source
